impacts.caseName: Dental Monitoring SAS v. Align Technology, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Board's Penumbra framework—holding that Dynamic Drinkware's written description analysis for provisional application priority dates applies only under pre-AIA law and not under AIA § 102(d)(2)—was correctly applied to determine prior art status of a reference patent.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the PTAB's obviousness determination and remanded, addressing the critical question of when a reference patent can claim the benefit of its provisional application's filing date for prior art purposes under the AIA. The court's resolution of the tension between Dynamic Drinkware and Penumbra has significant implications for how prior art dates are established in IPR proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent owners benefit from a potentially stricter standard for challengers seeking to establish earlier prior art dates through provisional applications, making it harder to invalidate patents in IPR proceedings.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies seeking to challenge patents in IPR proceedings may face greater difficulty establishing prior art status of references that rely on provisional application filing dates.

impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for method claims directed to treating headache with anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies permits broad genus claims where any member of the claimed genus would be effective for the recited treatment.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing on a panel decision upholding broad method-of-treatment patent claims for anti-CGRP antibodies, with Judge Dyk dissenting. The dissent argued the panel's holding is contrary to Supreme Court enablement precedent and will undermine medical innovation by sustaining overly broad claims. This case has major implications for pharmaceutical patent scope.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical and biotech patent holders benefit from the panel's more permissive enablement standard for method claims, allowing broader genus claims to survive challenges where functional limitations define the claimed antibodies.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic drug manufacturers and biosimilar competitors face broader blocking patents on methods of treatment, potentially delaying market entry and increasing litigation costs to challenge enablement.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the licensed patents such that the licensee could sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the licensee's shift to enforcement-only activities constituted cessation of business operations triggering automatic termination of the license.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal of a patent infringement suit, holding that the exclusive license agreement between Texas A&M University and TexasLDPC conveyed all substantial rights, making TexasLDPC effectively the patent owner with standing to sue independently. The court also held that shifting to enforcement activities did not constitute ceasing business operations under the agreement. This clarifies when exclusive licensees can enforce patents without joinder.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent licensing entities and exclusive licensees gain clarity that agreements conveying broad enforcement rights constitute effective assignments, allowing independent litigation without joining the patent owner.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a procedural defense of challenging standing based on non-joinder of the patent owner when facing suits from exclusive licensees with broad license agreements.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding trade secret damages testimony and vacating breach of contract jury awards in a case involving Ford's development of competing software after licensing Versata's automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, directing the district court to reconsider two damages models it had excluded. The court also reversed the district court's judgment on breach of contract damages and reinstated the jury award, while affirming trade secret misappropriation liability. This case provides important guidance on damages methodology in trade secret cases involving software.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software developers and licensors benefit from the reinstated breach of contract jury award and the opportunity for broader damages theories in trade secret cases, strengthening protections for proprietary software.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop competing products after licensing relationships face continued exposure to trade secret misappropriation liability and potentially larger damages on remand.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming non-uniform constellations for digital communications are eligible for patenting under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied judgment as a matter of law on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated patent eligibility for some asserted claims while affirming eligibility for others, affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, and remanded for further proceedings. The case provides significant guidance on the Alice § 101 framework as applied to digital communications technology standards, affecting how standard-essential patents are evaluated for eligibility.
impacts.positiveImplications: Technology companies implementing communications standards benefit from the partial vacatur of eligibility, potentially reducing royalty exposure for standard-essential patents found ineligible under § 101.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders asserting standard-essential patents face uncertainty as the court applied different eligibility outcomes to related claims, and must defend eligibility on remand for vacated claims.

impacts.caseName: Range of Motion Products, LLC v. Armaid Company Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Egyptian Goddess framework for design patent infringement improperly focuses on differences rather than overall similarity, and whether functionality determinations in design patent claim construction present jury questions.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing in a design patent case, with a divided court. The concurrence defended the Egyptian Goddess ordinary observer test, while the dissent (joined by four judges) argued the framework has improperly shifted the infringement inquiry toward differences and allowed courts to resolve infringement at summary judgment without adequate examination of prior art. This signals potential instability in design patent law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the current framework that permits summary judgment of non-infringement based on clear visual differences between claimed and accused designs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Design patent holders face continued risk that the Egyptian Goddess framework allows courts to dismiss infringement claims at summary judgment by focusing on dissimilarities, though the close en banc vote signals possible future reconsideration.

impacts.caseName: Board of Regents of the University of Texas System v. Boston Scientific Corp.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Boston Scientific was entitled to judgment as a matter of law of invalidity for anticipation and non-infringement of patents directed to drug-releasing biodegradable fiber implants used in coronary stent systems.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed a jury verdict in favor of the University of Texas, holding that Boston Scientific was entitled to JMOL of both invalidity by anticipation and non-infringement for patents covering drug-eluting stent technology. The court did not reach the cross-appeal on willfulness. This decision eliminates a significant patent liability for a major medical device manufacturer.
impacts.positiveImplications: Medical device manufacturers benefit from the reversal, which eliminates infringement liability and validates prior art defenses against university-owned patents in the coronary stent space.
impacts.negativeImplications: University patent holders and research institutions face the loss of infringement verdicts at JMOL stage, underscoring the vulnerability of composition patents to anticipation challenges.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient reasoning in denying Rule 11 sanctions and attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 where the patent holder had received multiple § 101 rejections of related applications before filing suit.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and fees, finding the court provided insufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent holder that filed infringement claims despite PTO § 101 rejections of related applications and a sister court's invalidation of a related patent. This decision strengthens the framework for deterring pursuit of likely-invalid patent claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from stronger appellate scrutiny of denials of fees and sanctions, which may deter patent holders from asserting patents with known § 101 vulnerabilities.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased risk of fee-shifting and sanctions when pursuing infringement claims involving patents with related applications that received § 101 rejections.

impacts.caseName: T-Mobile US, Inc. v. KAIFI LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Circuit has subject-matter jurisdiction over a dispute concerning the interpretation of a patent litigation settlement agreement's contingent payment clause tied to ex parte reexamination outcomes.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit held it lacked jurisdiction over a contract dispute about whether asserted claims 'survived' an ex parte reexamination, finding the dispute was purely a state-law contract interpretation issue that did not necessarily depend on resolving a substantial patent law question. The case was transferred to the Fifth Circuit. This clarifies jurisdictional boundaries for patent settlement agreement disputes.
impacts.positiveImplications: Parties to patent settlements benefit from clarity that contract disputes over settlement terms will be adjudicated in regional circuits applying state contract law, potentially yielding more predictable outcomes.
impacts.negativeImplications: Parties who structured settlement agreements expecting Federal Circuit review of patent-related payment triggers may face unexpected forum changes, requiring familiarity with regional circuit contract law.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims of a patent directed to a communications apparatus using a coupler to match impedance for transmitting signals 'over air' are invalid for lack of enablement under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), despite being found definite.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds. The court found the patent claims were not enabled because they claimed transmission of electromagnetic signals 'over air' using a coupler in a manner that was scientifically impossible as claimed. This provides important guidance on enablement as an independent validity defense.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from the affirmance of invalidity on enablement grounds, demonstrating that enablement can serve as a strong alternative defense even when indefiniteness arguments fail.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face risk that claims surviving indefiniteness challenges may still be invalidated for lack of enablement, particularly where claims implicate physical impossibilities.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the asserted claims of patents directed to crystalline forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) when the specification discloses the malate salt generally but does not specifically describe all claimed crystalline forms.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that Exelixis's cabozantinib malate salt patents have adequate written description, upholding patent protection for the cancer drug Cabometyx through 2030. This decision is commercially significant given Cabometyx's substantial market presence and the ongoing Hatch-Waxman litigation with generic challengers.
impacts.positiveImplications: Brand pharmaceutical companies benefit from the affirmance of written description adequacy for crystalline form patents, protecting revenue streams for blockbuster drugs against generic entry.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers face continued barriers to market entry as the court upheld patent validity, delaying access to lower-cost alternatives for cancer treatments.

impacts.caseName: VDPP, LLC v. Volkswagen Group of America, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court abused its discretion in denying leave to amend a patent infringement complaint, awarding attorney fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285, and sanctioning plaintiff's counsel under 28 U.S.C. § 1927.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal without leave to amend, fee award, and sanctions against plaintiff's counsel for bringing a frivolous patent infringement action. The court found the proposed amended complaint was futile and the case was exceptional under § 285. This reinforces the consequences for filing meritless patent suits and holds both patent owners and their attorneys accountable.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers benefit from robust enforcement of § 285 fee-shifting and § 1927 sanctions, which deter frivolous patent litigation and ensure recovery of defense costs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent assertion entities and patent litigation attorneys face heightened risk of fee awards and personal sanctions for pursuing infringement claims that lack adequate factual and legal support.

impacts.caseName: Archroma U.S., Inc. v. Department of Commerce
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether Commerce's regulatory 15-day deadline for domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in antidumping sunset reviews conflicts with the governing statute, which is silent on such deadlines.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade, holding that Commerce's regulation requiring domestic interested parties to indicate intent to participate in sunset reviews within 15 days is a permissible exercise of the agency's delegated authority. The statute is silent on timing, and the regulation was the product of reasoned decisionmaking. This preserves the existing procedural framework for antidumping duty review proceedings.
impacts.positiveImplications: Domestic manufacturers seeking to maintain antidumping protections benefit from clarity on the 15-day participation deadline, and the decision preserves Commerce's procedural authority to manage sunset reviews efficiently.
impacts.negativeImplications: Domestic producers who miss the 15-day deadline face potential revocation of antidumping duty orders, as Commerce's regulatory timeline has been upheld as valid despite the statute's silence on deadlines.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court correctly construed the term 'internal diameter' in oil and gas wellbore tool patent claims, and whether infringement and validity findings were supported.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's final judgment regarding infringement and validity of patents directed to float tools used in oil well casing operations. The dispute centered on the construction of 'internal diameter' in the claims, which has significant implications for patent coverage in the oil and gas equipment industry. The remand will require reconsideration of infringement and validity under the correct claim construction.
impacts.positiveImplications: Oil and gas equipment competitors benefit from the potential narrowing of patent scope on remand, which could open design-around opportunities for wellbore completion tools.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders in the oil and gas sector face uncertainty as claim construction disputes are remanded, potentially reducing the scope of protection for patented downhole tools.
